description:
Designs page plus a new design, the Robot Glove Hand.
(1) Designs tab in the Helping Hands app: one large card per project, each with its live 3D render right there (reuse the existing CAD viewer with rotate and explode/assemble), big enough to see from across the room. Order: 1. Gripper (the existing generations). 2. Robot Glove Hand (new, below). 3. The wearable capture device (voice-b3454864) once mocked up.
(2) Robot Glove Hand (OpenSCAD, generations kept as labeled files like the gripper): a robot hand that is hollow in the middle, an exoskeleton glove that Jake's own hand fits inside. His fingers go into the robot's fingers. The same hand is what the robot uses AND what Jake wears, so demonstrations are recorded on the robot's own joints. Mounting it on the robot arm works like putting on a glove: the arm's end has a hand-shaped mount or 'robot hand' core that slides in where Jake's hand would go. It needs enough empty space inside for an adult hand, assuming a large hand with margin, so it will be much bigger than the Aero Hand, and that's okay. Think about tendon or servo routing on the back of the hand so the inside stays clear, and a left-hand version to match the Aero. Ties into the glove-teaching plan (plans/aero-hand-glove-teaching.md) and the human-mirror principle.

results.notes: Jake sent the photo: cad/glove_hand/refs/jake_left_hand_spread_top.jpg. It shows his LEFT hand, palm down, fingers fully spread, on a wooden bench, with a tape measure (cm on the left edge, inches on the right) lying beside it on the same surface. The photo is taken roughly top-down from his eye, so correct for perspective. My rough read: about 24 px/cm at the tape; middle fingertip to wrist crease about 18 cm; pinky tip to thumb tip spread about 18 cm. Measure properly from the image. If thickness is needed, ask for finger widths (digital calipers are on his desk) or a side photo.

results.identified_issue: Latest human turn asks to start small: step 1 = outline from a top-down photo with a scale reference, TPU glove shell fitting the spread hand. No photo existed (hand.pdf at repo root = Aero assembly PDF, same 60 MB as ~/Downloads/Assembly_Instructions-*.pdf). Rather than only asking, built the extractor (PIL + numpy + scipy.ndimage + contourpy; no OpenCV installed): Otsu threshold, foreground = class touching the border less, largest blob = hand, second = card (PCA side ratio must be 1.35-1.85), wrist = narrowest row in bottom 40%, RDP 0.3 mm, CCW polygon. Chose a flat fit TRAY rather than a closed shell for gen_00: a closed shell needs thickness data we don't have, and its dorsal dome needs supports in TPU; the tray isolates the outline accuracy check. Untested on a real photo: shadows, skin/paper contrast, or a sleeve could break segmentation (fall back to --mm-per-px, or improve the threshold). Designs-tab (part 1 of the original description) deliberately deferred.
results.summary: Step 1 is ready for your photo. I built a photo-to-outline tool and a thin TPU fit tray that's generated from the outline. Please send a top-down photo of your spread hand with a credit card next to it.
results.detailed_description:
I didn't find a hand photo. hand.pdf in the repo and the newest file in ~/Downloads are both the Aero Hand assembly instructions. So I built the step-1 pipeline, and your photo can go straight in.

What I need from you: lay your LEFT hand fully spread, palm down, on plain white paper, fingers pointing to the top of the photo and wrist toward the bottom. Put a credit card flat on the paper, not touching your hand, and shoot straight down from about 50 cm. AirDrop it and I'll pick it up from ~/Downloads. For step 2 (the closed shell) I'll also need thickness: a side photo of the flat hand next to the card, or caliper widths and thicknesses of each finger at the middle knuckle plus palm thickness.

What I built (cad/openscad/glove_hand/):
- outline_from_photo.py turns the photo into the hand outline in mm (hand_outline.scad). It finds the card as the second-largest blob and uses its 85.6 mm long side as the scale. It cuts the outline at the wrist, the narrowest row in the bottom 40% of the hand. It also draws the outline back over the photo in red (outline_preview.png) so a bad trace is obvious. On a synthetic test photo with a known scale, the scale came out 0.17% off and the outline matched within its 0.3 mm simplification tolerance.
- gen_00_fit_tray.scad is your outline as one 0.8 mm TPU pad (the future palm and finger-pad layer) with an 8 mm wall around it, 1.5 mm clearance per side, and an open wrist end. It prints flat with no supports. Lay your spread hand in it: if every finger drops in without riding up the wall, the outline is right. It only tests width and finger angles, not thickness.

Caveat: hand_outline.scad currently holds a PLACEHOLDER: a synthetic large left hand I drew (about 95th-percentile male), not yours. The SCAD prints a warning while that's true, and I left out the STL so nobody prints it by mistake. The tray footprint is about 19 x 20 cm, so check that your printer bed fits it. I haven't started the Designs tab or the actual robot glove; per your note, those come after the shell fits.

results.notes:
Jake, design priority for the Robot Glove Hand: minimize the material between his hand and the object he grabs. The palm and finger pads should ideally be a single thin layer of TPU, so all actuation, cords and structure go on the back and sides, never under the fingers or palm. Start small:
Step 1: from a top-down photo of Jake's hand spread fully flat next to a scale reference (ruler or credit card), extract the outline. Build a 3D-printable TPU glove shell (OpenSCAD) that fits over the hand fully spread, so it captures the maximum width. Print, test the fit, iterate.
Step 2: once the shell fits, build the robot glove around it.
Ask Jake for the photo (he can AirDrop it; look in ~/Downloads), and add depth or thickness measurements as needed, e.g. a side photo or his measured finger widths.

user_request.name: mock it up in 3D and then add it to our designs page. I should be able to see each project quite large and then the actual render displayed right there. So the first project is the gripper, second project is the hand... like a robot glove... what both the robot uses and what I use... the hand is empty in the middle... sufficient to fit a hand in the center... the hand has to be a lot bigger. But that's okay.

summary: Build a Robot Glove Hand in OpenSCAD, starting with a thin TPU shell outlined from Jake's spread left-hand top-down photo using the tape measure for scale. The palm and finger pads must be a single thin TPU layer, with all actuation and structure on the back and sides.
